chunks.text: Let's dive into one of NextJS's core features, routing. NextJS uses a file system-based routing system, meaning the URLs you can access in your browser are determined by how you organize your files and folders in your code. Let me show you how this works with some

practical examples. I have created a new NextJS project using the command npx create-next-app@latest routing-demo. Routing-demo is the name of our project. When the command completes successfully, you should have a project similar to mine. Navigate to the source folder.

Now, we will start fresh by deleting the app folder, since we are going to build our routes from scratch. I mentioned earlier that NextJS has a file-based routing mechanism. You might naturally wonder, does every file in our app folder become a route? Not quite.

NextJS is built around conventions, and routing is one area where these conventions are particularly important. There are three main conventions to remember. First, all routes must live inside the app folder. Second, route files must be named either page.js or page.tsx, depending on whether you're

using TypeScript. Third, each folder represents a segment of the URL path. When these conventions are followed, the file automatically becomes available as a route. Let's put this into practice. For scenario one, we want to create a home page that shows up when someone

visits our site at localhost:3000. Let's head back to VS Code and implement the scenario. The first key convention in NextJS routing is that all routes must be placed in an app folder within the source directory. Let's create this folder. The second convention is that any file

meant to be a route must be named page.tsx or page.js if you're not using TypeScript. Let's create a page.tsx file in the app folder. From this file, we will default export a simple React component. Export default function home, and this returns an each one tag that says welcome home.

And just like that, we have created our first Next.js route. In the terminal, run the command npm run dev to start the dev server. In the browser, visit localhost:3000, and you will see welcome home displayed. This is our first key routing concept to remember. page.tsx file inside the app folder

automatically maps to your site's root URL. With that, we have successfully implemented scenario one. Before we continue, let's talk about the layout.tsx file. Even though we deleted this file when removing the app folder, Next.js will automatically create and

set it up when you first access the root route. We will explore layouts in depth later, but for now, just remember that this file gets automatically created behind the scenes. Now, let's tackle scenario number two. For this scenario, we need to create two additional routes, one for the about

page, and one for the profile page. The URL will read localhost:3000/about, and localhost:3000/profile. Back in VS Code, let's create these routes. There are three simple steps. First, create a new folder called about inside the app folder. Second, inside this about folder, create a page.tsx file.

Third, from this file, default export a React component. Export default function about, which returns an each one about me. Similarly, create yet another folder in the app folder called profile. Inside the folder, create a page.tsx file. From this file, default export a React

component. Export default function profile, return an H1 tag that says my profile. After saving the files and heading back to the browser, the home page will still be displayed at the root route, localhost:3000. When you navigate to localhost:3000/about, you will see the about me page, and

similarly, going to /profile will show the my profile page. Scenario two is now complete. The second key routing concept to remember is that routes are directly tied to their folder names within the app directory. A page.tsx file inside the about folder maps to the /about route, and a page.tsx

file inside the profile folder maps to the /profile route. Let me show you a quick visualization of everything we have covered so far. It is pretty straightforward. page.tsx in the app folder directly maps to the root route, and each folder in the app folder directly maps to a segment in your URL.

Now, you might be wondering what happens if someone tries to access a URL that doesn't match any file in your app folder. Let's say someone tries to visit /dashboard. In this case, Next.js has got you covered. It will automatically serve up a 404 not found response. You don't need

to write any special code to handle these non-existing routes. By now, you should have a solid understanding of how file-based routing works in Next.js. The beauty of this system is that you don't need to mess around with installing and configuring a router in your code. Your

file and folder structure does all the heavy lifting. This is a perfect example of Next.js's philosophy of favoring conventions over configuration when it comes to routing. All right, let's continue exploring more routing concepts. Supporting the channel is free. Please

Welcome to Build Bites Daily. Hey all you NextJS developers out there, you know that feeling when your static homepage just flies? It's instant, but then you click over to a blog post or a product page and there's that little bit of a delay. Well, in this explainer, we

are going to crush that delay. Yeah, this is probably one of the most common questions I see. You build this lightning fast site, but the performance just doesn't seem to hold up for your dynamic content. Don't worry, you are definitely not alone. And the good news

is there's a fantastic solution baked right into Nex.js. So let's talk about what's really going on here. So the whole issue really comes down to how dynamic routes are handled by default. I mean they're amazing, right? You can have one file like /slug.js that handles

all of your thousands of blog posts. But that flexibility comes with a hidden cost. That hidden cost is in those two words on demand. See, when a user asks for a dynamic page that hasn't been built yet, the server has to scramble. It has to wake up, go fetch the data,

actually render the HTML for the page, and only then can it send it back to the user. Every one of those steps takes time, and that's time your user is just staring at a loading screen. We can do way, way better than that. And that's, my friends, is where our hero of the day

comes in. Generate static params. This is a seriously powerful function in the Nex.js JS OP router that lets us completely change the game for our dynamic pages, turning that wait time into instant load time. The official docs really say it all. Instead of waiting for a user to show up and ask

for a page, we're going to proactively tell Nex.js, hey, build all these pages ahead of time when you're building the whole site. It's a huge shift, and it is the absolute key to unlocking that top tier performance. Honestly, the best way to wrap your head around this is to

think of it like you're handing Next.js JS, a to-do list or a shopping list. You're just saying, "Okay, before you deploy everything, I need you to go out and create a ready to go HTML page for product ID 1, product ID 2, and my blog post titled Hello World." So, what's the

result of giving Next.js that list? Well, every single one of those pages gets pre-built, packaged up, and sent to a CDN where it just sits there waiting. The moment a user clicks the link, bam, the page is served instantly. No server thinking, no on demand rendering, just

pure speed, just like your homepage. All right, so that all sounds great in theory, but how do we actually make this build list in our code? You'll be surprised at how simple and intuitive it actually is. Let's get into the nitty-gritty. Okay, at its core, the entire job of generate static params is

to do one thing, return an array. That's it. And inside that array, you put a bunch of little objects. Each one of those objects tells Nex.js JS about one single page you want it to pre-build. And what's so cool about this is how logical it is. The shape of the objects

you return has to match the dynamic parts of your URL. So if your URL has a dynamic ID, your object needs a key called ID. If your URL has category and product, well, your object needs keys for both. It just makes sense. Let's look at some real code. Okay, let's

start with the most basic case you can imagine. We have a route with just one dynamic segment ID. Inside our page.tsx file for that route. We just export our function and return an array of objects. Here we're returning three objects each with a different ID. And that's it.

We're literally telling Nex.js, when you build the site, please create static pages for /roduct 1/2 and/prouct/3. Done. So what if your URL is more complex? What if you have multiple dynamic parts? It's just as easy. For a route like / product/category/prouct, our objects just need to have keys for

both category and product. In this case, we're pre-building two very specific pages. Product one in category A and product two in category B. And yeah, of course, it works with those tricky catch all routes, too. For a route using dot dot dot slug, the only difference is

that the value for the slug key is an array of strings. Each string in that array becomes a segment in the final path. So, slug equals a1 perfectly generates the path / product/ a1. It's really flexible. Oh, and a super important pro tip here, especially for anyone coming from the old pages router.

If you're thinking, hm, this sounds a lot like get static paths, you're exactly right. Generate static params is the new modern replacement for get static paths in the app router. Same job, new name. Okay, so hard- coding an array like that is perfect for understanding how this works. But in a

real world app, you're not going to sit there and type out the IDs for 500 blog posts. Your data is coming from somewhere else. So let's look at how we can generate these paths dynamically. The most common approach is to just build everything up front. You can make generate static params and async

function, which is awesome. This lets you await a fetch call to your database or your CMS right inside the function. You grab all your posts and then just use a simple map to transform that list of posts into the array of params objects that Nex.js JS needs. This is

perfect for your typical blog or doc site where you want every single page to be static and instant. But what if you have an e-commerce store with 50,000 products? Building all of those pages at once could make your build times really, really long. So a much smarter strategy

is to just build a subset. For instance, you could fetch all your products, but only return the params for, say, your top 100 best sellers. Those 100 pages will be instant. What about the other 49,900? They'll get generated on demand the very first time someone visits them

and then they'll be cached. It's truly the best of both worlds. And then there's this third really cool option, build absolutely nothing at build time. You can just return an empty array. You're telling Nex.js, hey, don't pre-build any of these pages. This means

every dynamic page will be generated on demand when it's requested for the first time and then cached. This powerful pattern is known as incremental static regeneration or ISR where your site builds itself over time as it's needed. Now, talking about these different

strategies brings up a really important question. What happens when a user tries to visit a URL that we didn't pre-build? Well, Nex.js gives us a very clear way to control exactly that behavior. That control comes from a little configuration option called dynamic

params. You just export it as a variable from your page file right alongside the function. This one setting tells NexJSJS exactly what to do with those unknown or ungenerated paths. And you've got two settings. The default is true. This means if a page wasn't pre-built, Nex.js

will try to generate it when it's requested. This is perfect for that subset strategy we just talked about. On the other hand, you can set dynamic params to false. This is like telling Nex.js, if the page isn't in my pre-built list, it simply does not exist. Period. Any request for a page

that wasn't pre-built will get a 404 error. And just a quick final tidbit you should know, the function behaves a little differently in development versus production. When you're running NextDev, it runs every time you navigate to a page so you can see your changes live.

But in production, it only runs one time during the next build command to generate all those static files for your deployment. All right, that was a lot of info. Let's just zoom out for a second and recap the big benefits here. Why should you really go to the trouble of

using this in your apps? First, and this is the big one, performance. Your users get that instant, snappy experience. Second, SEO. Google and other search engine crawlers absolutely love plain HTML files. They can index your site so much faster. Third, you're taking a huge

load off your server since it's not constantly having to build pages. And finally, your builds become way more reliable and predictable. You know exactly what pages are going to exist when you hit deploy. So that brings me to my question for you. I want you to think about the projects you're working

on right now. Is it a blog, an e-commerce site, a portfolio? Which one of your dynamic routes could you give a massive speed boost to with generate static params? What pages can you take from on demand and make instant? That's the challenge I'm leaving you with. If

you found this explainer useful and it helps clear things up, please do me a favor and hit that like and subscribe button for more deep dives into web development right here on Build Bites Daily. Thanks for watching and happy coding.

chapters.label: How To Nest Server And Client Components

chunks.text: If you've ever written code in React, you know how painful it is—seeing those long useEffects on the left with fetch queries, state management, and other complexities, just to get data and render the page . Fortunately, with the new ideology of server-side components

promoted by React, this will be a thing of the past. It allows you to write a simple file like the one you see on the right , which uses modern JavaScript concepts and replaces everything on the left much more easily. So, in this video, I'll explain in detail what server-side components are and

compare them to client-side components in React. Welcome back to WebDev Simplified. My name is Kyle, and my job is to simplify the web for you so you can start building your dream project faster. Today I want to talk about the difference between client-side and server-side components. If you've

heard of client and server components, you might think this is a feature of Next.js. In fact, this is a feature of React itself, and Next.js simply implements them in its own, specific way. In this video, I will be using server-side components in the context of Next.js, as you can see on the left of

the screen. In the future, this will be possible in many frameworks , but for now, Next.js has the most robust support for server-side components. By the way, if you prefer text-based tutorials, I have a full blog article on the same topic. I will leave a link to it

in the description below. There are over 100 articles on the blog , so I highly recommend checking them out. The basic idea behind server-side components is that for client-side components, you usually need to execute all your code on the client side. Everything is rendered on

the client, which means having to create long and confusing useEffects to get all the necessary data from some API. So now you need to develop both the API and the frontend, which becomes quite complicated. The idea of server components is that we can execute code on the server: make fetch

requests directly in the code and immediately return the necessary data. Instead of sending HTML and JavaScript , then making a request to the API, and then retrieving the data—this two-step process is no longer necessary. Server components do all this in one step. This is how it works: server

components only run on the server. They are never executed on the client. This is very easy to see. If we just go here and add a simple console log that says "server ", and here we add a console log that says "client". We will be able to see exactly where these entries appear

in the console. So, I'll update my page right here. This is a client page. If I check the page, go to the console, I see that it prints "client" many times in my vine. You can see it right here . Now, if I go to my server page and refresh it a few times, you'll notice that

nothing is output in this console . But if I open the console of my project, you will notice that every time I refresh the page, it displays "server". This means that this server component only runs on the server. And again , if I check the page on the client, you'll notice that no matter

how many times I refresh, nothing appears in the console . Interesting point: when I go to my client page, nothing actually re-renders. But when the page is fully refreshed, it actually renders my client component on the server. This is a feature of the implementation of client-side

components in Next.js: when you first navigate to a page with a client-side component, it is launched on the server for SEO purposes. But again, this is a Next.js feature, not React. That's the big difference between these two components. By ensuring that our server component is never executed on

the client, we can do a few interesting things. First and foremost, we can make this component asynchronous. As you can see, I made this an asynchronous function , which means I can directly use await for fetch requests, database queries, or anything else that takes time, and just render the code

afterwards. So I don't have to worry about loading states, errors, use effects for queries, or state management—all of this is handled by a simple async await, just like in regular JavaScript code. And this makes it much closer to regular JavaScript, and also greatly simplifies the process of

understanding and reading the code. Now you can still handle loading and error states. In Next.js, this simply requires creating a load file or error file directly here. And if you want to learn more about specific ways to work with them in Next.js, I have a full video course on Next.js. I

will leave a link to it in the cards and description. But for this video, it doesn't matter, as we're focusing on the server-side components. So, the advantage of doing all this on the server is the added layer of security. This is because no piece of code in my server component that relies on

database calls or certain API credentials is passed to the client. For example, if in this fetch request I needed to pass sensitive information to the API, I would simply add it, say, to the body of the request, where I would specify the secret data, regardless of what it is. This secret data

will never be visible on the client side of the page, as all this code is executed on the server, and only what I return here is sent to the client. So, only the plain HTML is sent, not the actual code that performs these fetch requests. This means that if I wanted to replace this

with, for example, db.todos.get or another way of retrieving tasks from the database, I could do so, with all my credentials remaining on the server and the client only receiving the retrieved information. That is, the tasks themselves and the corresponding HTML code. The next huge

benefit of server-side components is performance, and there are three different ways they improve the performance of your application. Let's return everything to the state where we executed the query. We will remove all this secret data to leave only the working code. And one of the

important features we can use is caching. Next.js has built-in caching by default, but even without Next.js, you can configure caching yourself . Since this cache is located on your server, it means that it is available to every user who visits your website. This means that you can directly

cache any HTML needed for that page based on my actions, and every user who visits my page will be able to access the same cache, and therefore everything will run extremely fast for all of them. If you were using a client component and wanted to cache something on the client side, it would

only be available to that one individual user . So instead you would need to do caching at the API level, i.e. create a cache where the request is sent from and then just send empty HTML. After that, they need to query that cache to get the information. In our case, having a server-side component,

we do everything in one step, which means that instead of sending empty data and a subsequent request, we simply send the finished HTML. This is one holistic process. Another big advantage of server-side components is that if you use code that runs on the server and is imported,

for example, from very large libraries, then this code remains only on the server, which significantly reduces the size of the JavaScript bundle sent to the client . Let's take a look at this library, for example. Let's say we have a very large file here. Sure, it's not very big, but imagine it's a

massive library of three or four megabytes. She is huge. And we want to use it in our server and client components. So, I'm going to go in here and import this function. I called it big funk. That's it. So we import it here . We'll do the same thing in our client component, like this. Now, if I go

to the client page and check the content, refresh the page, I'll notice that if I open the source code and use Ctrl + Shift + F to search for " big funk," I'll see that line everywhere in the code because it's become part of the output of my client component. Now, if I go to my server page and do a

quick full refresh, and then do the same search—go to the source code, find “big funk,” and hit “search”—no matches are found. This is because this code only runs on the server, which means all of this huge file import never makes it to the client, which significantly reduces the amount of code

I ship. Whereas when using the client component, standard for React, everything I import here must be sent to the client. The last performance benefit is perhaps the most obvious: your page will load faster overall. This is because instead of sending a client component, making a request to retrieve

data, and processing all that information on the client, I do it all in one step on the server. The client sends a request, the server executes it and returns the finished HTML with all my data. So you never have to worry about incomplete data on the client or similar issues. You get everything you

need right away, which is very convenient and usually works faster. Finally, a significant advantage of server-side components over client-side ones is that they are usually better for SEO. The reason is that the server sends ready-made HTML, fully populated with your information, while the client

component sends only partially formed HTML. And then it needs to use things like ` useEffect` to fill in the rest of the information. Of course, search engines have learned to work better with this, and you can use server-side rendering tools in React, but with server-side components it's

much easier and built in automatically. Given all these benefits, you might think: why not make everything server- side? The reason is that since your code is never executed on the client, you won't be able to add any interactivity to the page. For example, let's say I want to add a

click event handler here. I could write ` on-click console.log hi`. That's all. And immediately I get a bunch of errors. This is because I can't use interactivity. I can't add click event handlers or any other types of event handlers. I can't use, for example, the ` useEffect` hook

. These are the things. If I add a use effect hook, like this. And I'll just try to run it. Right away, if I try to import this, the effects from React, and save it, I get an error again because I can't use use effect. I can't use, for example, use state. You can't use any hooks inside a server

component. And this is again because you cannot implement interactivity. So it's very important that if you have any interactivity on the page, it should be inside the client-side component. But because of the incredible benefits of server-side components, I usually try to make as many of my

components server-side as possible, and only in the few places where I really need interactivity do I use client-side ones. And I just make sure that all the data that I need, like any tasks that need to be retrieved, comes from the server component and is passed into this client

component as a prop, like this . Another big downside: since your server component is never rendered on the client, you can't use things like local storage or anything else from the window object, because that simply doesn't exist in the server environment, and it never runs on the client. So

things like local storage, navigator, or any other browser API cannot be used inside a server component. Although these are almost all the disadvantages of server components. The only other important question is how to embed server components into client components and vice versa? Because

right now, if I wanted to, inside my server component, I could go down here and render some client component. It doesn't matter what it is, it will work perfectly fine. All of this code will be rendered on the server, and then this particular client component will be rendered on the client. Now,

the way to define a component as client-side in Next.js, at least, is to add the line "use client" at the very beginning of the file, and that's Next.js' way of indicating that it's going to be a client-side component. So, I can place client components inside server components without any

problems. But once I have a client-side component, like this one , all the child elements of that component also become client-side, regardless of whether I marked them as client-side, they will only render on the client, not on the server. So, you essentially only have one attempt to switch from

server to client, and after that you can never go back. For example, in this client component, I will never be able to render the server component because I have already switched to the client and can no longer go back to the server. This is essentially a one-way ticket. But there

is one way to get around this. To show what I'm talking about, I'll just create a completely new file. So, we'll place it in this components folder. Let 's create this file and name it client.tsx. We export the client function like this. And it will return an H1 with the text "client" so

we know that this is being rendered on the client. And internally, I'm just going to simplify it a lot by rendering this client-side component. It's important that internally I make sure this works on the client by adding "use client" at the very beginning. So now this code is rendered on

the client and this one is rendered on the server, which means if I put a console log here that says " client," you'll notice that when you check in the console, it's outputted right there. So from now on, everything inside will be a client-side component, and even if I render another component, it

will also render on the client. But what if I want to render something on the server inside this component? Well, I need to actually pass it as a prop from the server component. So let me create another component here. I'll call it server.tsx. We export the server function. And it

will look almost the same. I'll just copy this code, paste it here, and replace "client" with "server." You'll notice right away if I refresh the page and render this component here. That's it. I'll make sure I imported this component. I'll save the changes quickly. You can see that we have a

client and a server rendering. And importantly, since this client component is rendered on the client, everything inside it, including this component that we called server-side, is also rendered on the client, which means that the console shows the server rendering on the client. And what

happens if this server component performs some data sampling? For example, it gets all these different tasks and I want to render that as an asynchronous component so that it happens directly on the server. Well, to do this and get around the limitation, I need to pass this component into my client

component as a prop. So, here I can pass the child element in any convenient way. I can pass it as a child element like this , or I can just render this server-side component by importing it. Thus, we pass it on as prop. Now here I can get these child elements and render them. You can simply

ignore the errors. This is just because I use TypeScript. So we'll define it as any. That's it. Now, if I save everything and refresh the page, you'll notice that the console no longer outputs "server" because this file is now being rendered on the server. And all because wherever you

import the file, it is executed there. In our case, we import this file into a server component, so it runs on the server. Whereas in the previous case, we imported it into a client file, so it was executed on the client. Since we import it here, it executes the entire server component

and then passes the result to this client component. So, if you want to go from server to client and then back to server, this is the only way to do it. But, to be honest, the need to do something like this doesn't arise that often . And when such a need arises, it does not become a big

inconvenience. However, it 's worth remembering that other frameworks may work slightly differently. This is the Next.js approach, and in many ways it overlaps with the React approach. But now the lines between Next.js and React are very blurred. Therefore, it is difficult to say whether all

chunks.text: [music] All right. Hey everyone, welcome back to the lang chain by project series. And today we're building something that feels genuinely smart. An AI that doesn't just answer your question. It actually checks its own answer, judges the quality, and fixes itself if it's wrong.

This is one of those projects where you immediately understand the power of Langchain. You ask a question, the AI responds. Another part of the AI reviews the response. And if it fails the check, a third step improves it automatically. All three steps, generation, evaluation,

and repair, run right on your laptop through Llama and Streamlit. So, let's jump straight into the code and see how this entire self-correcting system is built. We start with the imports. We import Streamlit because that's the UI layer. We import optional from typing

for a helper function later. Then we bring in chat Olama from the lang chain community package. This is what connects us to the local llama model running in Olama. We also import chat prompt template to build prompts and stream output parser to convert the model's responses into plain text.

Next, we define the model name. Here we are using Llama 3.23B. This must match a model that already exists in your Olama installation. Then we configure the streamlit page with a title and a wide layout. After that, we set up the model. We create the LLM object using chatma passing the

model name and a temperature of 0.4. Lower temperature means cleaner, more controlled answers. We also create the parser object using stream output parser which converts the output into simple text. Now we create the prompts for the three stages of our pipeline. The first one is

the generation prompt. This prompt tells the AI to be helpful, answer clearly and respond to whatever input the user provides. It has one placeholder called input where the user's question will go. The second prompt is the evaluation prompt. This part of the AI acts like a

reviewer. We give it the original question and the AI's answer. Then we ask it to judge the answer on correctness, clarity, and completeness. And most importantly, it must reply in a fixed format. It either says pass followed by a short explanation or fail followed by what is wrong and why. This

strict format is important because the rest of the pipeline depends on it. The third prompt is the repair prompt. This one only runs if the evaluation step fails. It gets the original question, the incorrect response, and the reviewer's feedback. and its job is

simple. Rewrite the answer so it becomes correct, clear, and complete. Once the prompts are ready, we turn each one into a chain by piping the prompt into the model and then into the parser. So, we end up with a generation chain, an evaluation chain, and a repair chain.

Next, we define a small helper function called get text. This function makes sure that no matter what shape the model returns, whether it returns an object or just a string, we extract clean text from it. It checks if the response has a content attribute. If it does, we return

that content. If not, we convert the entire object to text. This keeps everything safe and predictable. Then we create the sidebar. The sidebar has a title that says guardrail controls. It has a checkbox that lets the user choose whether the system should automatically repair failed

answers. By default, auto repair is turned on. Below that, we show a small info box explaining that this episode demonstrates self- evaluation, guardrails, and conditional repair, all running locally. Now we move to the main interface. We set the main title to episode 11 self-correcting AI system.

that stands for Term Frequency Inverse Document Frequency. TF-IDF highlights words that are frequent within a specific document, but are rare across the entire corpus. So, for example, in a document about coffee, TF-IDF would emphasize words like espresso or cappuccino, which might appear often

in that document, but rarely in others about different topics. Common words like the or and, which appear frequently across all documents, would receive low TF-IDF based scores. Now another embedding type is called prediction based embeddings and prediction based embeddings.

They capture semantic relationships and contextual information between words. So, for example, in the sentences, "the dog is barking loudly." and "the dog is wagging its tail." A prediction based model would learn to associate dog with words like bark, wag, and tail.

This allows these models to create a single fixed representation for dog that encompasses various, well, dog related concepts. Prediction based embeddings. They excel at separating words with close meanings, and can manage the various senses in which a word may be used.

Now there are various models for generating word embeddings. One of the most popular is called word2vec that was developed by Google in 2013. Now word2vec has two main architectures. There's something called c b, o, w and there's something called skip-gram, and CBOW, that's an acronym

for Continuous Bag of Words. Now CBOW predicts a target word based on its surrounding context words. Well, skip-gram does the opposite, predicting the context words given a target word. Now another popular method is called GLOVE.

Also an acronym, that one stands for Global Vectors for Word Representation. That was created at Stanford University in 2014 and that uses co-occurrence statistics to create word vectors. Now, these models, they differ in their approach. What's a vec that focuses on learning from

the immediate context around each word? While glove takes a broader view by analyzing how often words appear together across the entire corpus, then uses this information to create word vectors. Now, while these two word embedding models continue to be valuable tools in NLP, the field has seen some

significant advances with the emergence of new tech, particularly transformers. While traditional word embeddings assign a fixed vector to each word, transformer models use a different type of embedding, and it's called a contextual based embedding. Now, contextual based embeddings are where

the representation of a word changes based on its surrounding context. So, for example, in a transformer model, the word bank would have different representations in the sentence I'm going to the bank to deposit money and I'm sitting on the bank of a river. This context sensitivity

allows these models to capture more nuanced meanings and relationships between words, which has led to all sorts of improvements in the various fields of NLP tasks. So that's word embeddings, from simple numeric vectors to complex representations.

Word embeddings have revolutionized how machines understand and process human language. Proving that transforming words into numbers is indeed a powerful tool for making sense of our linguistic world.

How modern RAG pipelines are solving the LLM hallucination problem. Introduction. Imagine asking an AI assistant a simple question about a court case and it confidently gives you a detailed answer complete with citations, quotes, and page numbers. The only problem? None of

it is real. The case doesn't exist. The quotes were invented. This isn't a hypothetical. It's happened to lawyers, students, and businesses around the world and it has a name, hallucination. For the last few years, hallucination has been the single biggest obstacle

standing between large language models and real-world trust. You can't put a model into a hospital, a courtroom, or a financial system if it sometimes just makes things up with total confidence. But here's the good news. Over the past 2 years, a technique called retrieval

augmented generation, RAG, has evolved from a simple trick into a sophisticated engineering discipline that is dramatically reducing hallucination rates. In this video, we're going to go deep into how modern RAG pipelines actually work, why they help, where they still fail, and what the cutting edge

looks like right now. By the end of this video, you'll understand the full anatomy of a production-grade RAG system from chunking and embeddings to hybrid retrieval, reranking, self-correction loops, and grounded generation. Let's get into it. Why do LLMs hallucinate?

Before we can appreciate the solution, we need to understand the disease. Large language models are at their core next token predictors. During training, they read enormous amounts of text and learn statistical patterns about which word is likely to follow another given the context so far.

There's no internal database of verified facts sitting inside the model. There's no lookup table. Everything the model knows is compressed into billions of numerical weights. And when you ask it a question, it's essentially performing an extremely sophisticated form of pattern completion.

This creates three distinct failure modes. The first is what researchers call parametric knowledge gaps. If a fact wasn't well represented in training data, or if it happened after the model's training cutoff, the model has no reliable way to know that it doesn't know. It will often still

generate a fluent, confidence-sounding answer because fluency is what it was trained to produce, not necessarily truthfulness. The second failure mode is what's sometimes called exposure bias, or more informally, the model's tendency to prioritize plausible-sounding

continuations over factually verified ones. Since training rewards the model for producing text that resembles its training distribution, a well-formed but false sentence can score just as well internally as a well-formed true one. The third mode is context drift in long

conversations, where the model gradually loses track of what's actually been established versus what it's inferring, and starts blending the two together. Now, here's the key insight that makes RAG so powerful. A huge portion of hallucination isn't a reasoning failure.

It's a knowledge access failure. The model isn't being irrational. It simply doesn't have the right facts in front of it, so it fills the gap using its general priors. If you could somehow hand the model the exact right passage of text right before it answers, a huge

fraction of these hallucinations simply disappear. That single insight is the entire foundation of retrieval augmented generation. The core idea of RAG. At its simplest, RAG works in two stages: retrieve, then generate. Before the language model writes a single word

of its answer, a separate retrieval system searches through an external knowledge source. This could be a company's internal documents, a medical database, Wikipedia, or the live web, and pulls out the passages most relevant to the user's question. Those passages are then inserted into the model's

prompt, essentially saying, "Here is some trustworthy, up-to-date information. Use this to answer the question." This sounds simple, but the engineering underneath it is where the real progress has happened. The first challenge is, how do you search over millions or

billions of documents fast enough to be useful? The classic solution is to convert text into embeddings, long lists of numbers that represent the meaning of a piece of text in a high-dimensional space. Two pieces of text that mean similar things end up as vectors that

are close together in that space, even if they don't share any of the same words. Once documents are embedded, they're stored in what's called a vector database. When a user asks a question, that question is also converted into an embedding, and the system searches for

the document vectors that are closest to the question's vector, typically using a similarity measure like cosine similarity. The idea behind that formula is straightforward, even though the math looks intimidating. It measures the angle between two vectors, and vectors pointing in nearly

the same direction get a high similarity score, regardless of their length. This retrieval step transforms the LLM from a closed-book exam taker into an open-book one. Instead of relying purely on memorized, potentially stale, potentially fuzzy knowledge, the model gets to read the

relevant material right before answering, dramatically increasing the odds that its answer is grounded in something real. But, and this is important, early RAG systems from a few years ago were fairly naive. They chunked documents into arbitrary fixed-size blocks, retrieved the top few

matches, and stuffed them into the prompt. That basic approach helped, but it still hallucinated plenty because retrieval itself can fail in subtle ways. The rest of this video is about how modern pipelines fix those subtle failures. Smarter chunking and indexing. One of the most underrated fixes in

modern RAG pipelines is simply getting smarter about how documents are broken into pieces, or chunks, before they're indexed. Early systems just split text every few hundred words, regardless of whether that cut a sentence, a table, or an idea in half. If a chunk boundary lands in the middle

of an important explanation, the retrieval system might only grab half the story and the model, trying to be helpful, fills in the missing half with a guess. That guess is a hallucination in disguise. Modern pipelines use what's called semantic chunking, where the text is

split at natural boundaries, the end of a paragraph, a section header, or a shift in topic. Often detected by measuring how much the meaning changes from one sentence to the next. Some systems go further with hierarchical indexing, where you don't just index small chunks, but also index

summaries of larger sections and summaries of summaries above that. This lets the retrieval system zoom in or out, similar to how a human might first find the right chapter of a book, then the right paragraph. Another major improvement is metadata-aware retrieval. Instead of treating every chunk as

anonymous text, modern systems attach metadata, the source document, the publication date, the author, the section title, and use that metadata to filter and re-rank results. This matters enormously for avoiding a specific type of hallucination, outdated information being presented as current.

If a system can filter to only documents published in the last 6 months, it avoids confidently citing a policy that was replaced last year. Finally, there's the idea of contextual chunk embeddings, a technique where, instead of embedding a chunk in isolation, the system embeds it together

with a short summary of the whole document it came from. This solves a subtle but common problem. A chunk that says, "The interest rate was reduced by half a percent" is meaningless on its own. Reduced from what? By whom? When? Contextual embedding bakes in just

enough surrounding information, so the retrieval system understands what the chunk is really about, even out of context. Dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval. There's a second major axis of improvement, how the actual matching between a question and a document happens.

Pure embedding-based search, often called dense retrieval, is excellent at understanding meaning and paraphrase. If you ask about a car that runs without gasoline, it can find documents about electric vehicles, even though the words don't overlap. But dense retrieval has a

weakness. It can struggle with very specific, rare terms, product codes, legal statute numbers, exact names, because those specific tokens can get diluted in a dense vector representation. That's where sparse retrieval comes back in. Older algorithms like BM25, which score

documents based on exact keyword overlap and term frequency, are still extremely good at pinpointing exact matches. The idea behind these scoring formulas is that a term which appears frequently in a specific document, but rarely across the whole collection, is a strong

signal that this document is highly relevant to a query containing that term. Modern RAG pipelines don't choose one or the other. They combine both in what's called hybrid retrieval. The system runs a dense semantic search and a sparse keyword search in parallel,

then merges the two ranked lists using a fusion method. One popular approach being reciprocal rank fusion, where each document gets a score based on how high it ranked in each individual list, and documents that rank well in both lists rise to the top. This hybrid approach captures the best

of both worlds, the conceptual understanding of dense vectors and the precision of exact keyword matching. This matters directly for hallucination because a huge class of factual errors comes from retrieval simply missing the right document, not because the generation model reasoned poorly, but

because the search step never found the needle in the haystack in the first place. If the right passage never makes it into the prompt, no amount of clever prompting will save you. Improving retrieval quality is, in a very real sense, improving truthfulness at the source.

Reranking and context curation. Retrieval gets you a short list of candidate documents, but not all of them are equally useful, and cramming too many into the prompt creates its own problems. This is where reranking comes in, a second, more computationally expensive,

but more accurate model that takes the initial candidates and rescores them by actually reading the query and each candidate together, rather than comparing precomputed vectors. These are often called cross-encoders because the query and document are encoded jointly, letting the model

directly compare fine-grained details, rather than relying on a rough geometric distance. Why does this matter for hallucination? Because there's a well-documented phenomenon called lost in the middle. Research has shown that language models pay the most attention to information

placed at the very beginning or the very end of their context window and tend to under weight information buried in the middle even when that middle information is highly relevant. If your retrieval system dumps 10 mediocre passages into the prompt with the one truly relevant passage buried at

position six the model may effectively fail to use it and hallucinate an answer instead. Modern pipelines address this with careful context curation, re-ranking to promote the most relevant passages, deduplication to remove near identical redundant chunks, and deliberate

placement strategies that put the most important information at the positions the model attends to most. Some systems also implement a relevance threshold. If the top retrieved documents all score below a certain confidence level the system doesn't force-feed them to the model at all.

Instead, it triggers a fallback response acknowledging that no sufficiently relevant information was found. This single design choice, being willing to say I don't have enough information is one of the most powerful hallucination reduction techniques there is because it directly targets the

model's tendency to always attempt a fluent answer regardless of whether it actually has the goods. Self-correcting and agentic RAG The most exciting frontier in RAG right now isn't just about retrieving better. It's about giving the system the ability to critique and correct itself before

the answer ever reaches the user. This family of techniques is often called self-RAG or corrective RAG and it works a bit like giving the model an internal editor. Here's how it works conceptually. After the initial retrieval, instead of immediately generating a final answer,

the system generates a draft answer along with an internal judgment. Does this retrieved context actually support this claim? If the system detects that a retrieved passage is irrelevant or that its own draft answer includes a claim not backed by any passage, it doesn't just ship that answer.

It can trigger one of several corrective actions. Retrieve again with a reformulated query. Search a different knowledge source entirely, including in some architectures, falling back to a live web search if the internal database comes up empty. Or simply strip out the

unsupported claim before finalizing the response. This turns RAG from a single-pass pipeline into an iterative loop, sometimes visualized as retrieve, generate, critique, and if necessary, retrieve again. Some of the most advanced systems now use what's called a gentic RAG, where

the language model itself acts as an orchestrator, deciding in real time which knowledge sources to query, how many retrieval rounds are needed, and when it has gathered sufficient evidence to answer confidently. This is a meaningful shift. Instead of a fixed pipeline designer deciding in

advance exactly how retrieval will happen, the model plans its own investigation, much like a researcher deciding to check just one more source before writing a conclusion. The hallucination reduction impact here is significant because it adds a verification layer that specifically

targets the moment where hallucination is born. The instant the model is about to state something it isn't actually sure about. Instead of that uncertainty silently becoming a confident sounding sentence, the system has a built-in checkpoint asking, "Is this actually grounded?"

Grounding, citations, and verification layers. The final piece of the puzzle is making the model's reasoning visible and checkable rather than a black box. Modern RAG systems increasingly require the model to attribute every factual claim to a specific retrieved passage,

essentially forcing inline citations as part of the generation process itself, not bolted on afterward. This has a subtle but powerful side effect. A model that has to point to exactly which passage supports a sentence is far less likely to write an unsupported sentence in the first place

because the citation requirement acts as a constant built-in self-check during generation. On top of that, many production systems now add a dedicated post-generation verification step. After the answer is drafted, a separate checking pass, sometimes another LLM call, sometimes a

specialized classifier, compares each sentence in the answer against the retrieved passages and flags any statement that isn't actually supported. Think of it as a fact-checking desk that reviews the article before it's published. If unsupported claims are found, the

system can either delete them, rephrase them as explicitly uncertain, or trigger another retrieval round. Together, these grounding techniques close the loop. Retrieval finds the facts, chunking and hybrid search make sure the right facts are found, re-ranking makes sure they're

prioritized correctly. Agentic self-correction catches gaps in real-time and citation-based verification acts as the final safety net before the answer reaches the user. No single layer is perfect on its own, but stacked together, they've moved RAG systems from helpful but unreliable to

something increasingly close to genuinely trustworthy for high-stakes use cases. Limitations, open challenges, and closing. Now, it's worth being honest. RAG is not a silver bullet. Retrieval can still fail if the underlying knowledge base is incomplete, biased, or itself contains

errors. Garbage in, garbage out still applies. Multi-hop questions, where the answer combines facts from several different documents in a chain of reasoning, remain genuinely difficult because a single retrieval pass might miss one crucial link in that chain. And there's an ongoing tension between

adding more verification layers and keeping response times fast enough for a good user experience. Every extra check adds latency. But the trajectory is unmistakable. What started as just paste some search results into the prompt has evolved into a genuinely sophisticated discipline

combining information retrieval, self-critique, and structured verification. The systems we've walked through today, semantic chunking, hybrid dense sparse search, cross-encoder re-ranking, self-correcting agentic loops, and citation-based grounding represent the current state of the art in making

language models not just fluent, but actually trustworthy. If you found this breakdown useful, consider subscribing for more deep dives into how modern AI systems really work under the hood. And let me know in the comments, have you run into an AI hallucination in the
wild? I'd love to hear your story. Thanks for watching and I'll see you in the next one.

chunks.text: we live in a world that runs on data it's how Amazon and Netflix know which movies and products to recommend how Starbucks manages a global supply chain and how Uber connects drivers with passengers in real time but the thing is data skills aren't just for tech companies or professional analysts

anymore everyone works with data to some degree and everyone can benefit from data literacy skills in this video we're covering an important topic that will help you take your data literacy to the next level when it comes time to decide how to visualize a data set or which specific

chart to use it's important to ask yourself three key questions number one what type of data are you working with is it geospatial time series categorical hierarchical or something more specialized number two what exactly do you want to communicate are you showing a comparison a composition a

relationship or a distribution and number three Who is the audience and what they need are you sharing this with an analyst a manager executive or the general public how you answer these questions will help you determine which type of chart or visual is most appropriate given the context so let's

unpack each of these in a bit more detail so question one what type of data are you working with there are many flavors of data out there including common ones like time series geospatial categorical and hierarchical but you might might also come across some more

unique and specialized types of data as well like financial statements textual data funnel stages survey responses and much much more and the key takeaway here is that the type of data you're working with often helps determine which type of visual will best represent it some

common examples include using maps for geospatial analysis line charts to show time series and bar or column charts for categorical comparisons other more specialized examples include things like waterfall charts to track Financial balances ler scales to summarize survey

responses even word clouds to visualize information from text-based documents question two is all about understanding what you want to communicate whether it's a comparison composition distribution or relationship comparison visuals as the name suggests are used to compare values over time or

across categories common visuals here include variations of bar and column charts along with line or area charts for showing time series and some less common examples might be something like a funnel chart if you specifically want to show sequential stages like for

example the number of applicants who made it through each round of a hiring process composition visuals are used to break down the component parts of a hole this is where you'll typically use stacked bar or column charts pies and donuts stacked area charts for showing

composition changes over time and maybe things like tree Maps or sun sunbursts if you're dealing with hierarchical data specifically distribution visuals are useful when you want to show the frequency of values within a series like the Olympic Athlete example we talked

about earlier in this course by far the most common and effective visual for showing distributions is the histogram but there are others as well like box and whisker charts density plots violin charts or heat maps and last but not least relationship visuals help you show

correlation between multiple variables this is typically done using Scatter Plots or variations like bubble charts but you might also use tools like a heat map or correlation Matrix to show a relationship as well now you might be feeling a little bit lost or overwhelmed

given just how many types of visuals exist but let me give you some peace of mind 90% of the time basic variations of bar column and line charts will be the simplest and clearest way to visualize your data so keep it simple avoid using complex or custom visuals unless you

absolutely need to and make sure to prioritize Simplicity and Clarity over Aesthetics and design that takes us to our third question who is the audience and what they need one of the most common mistakes that we see people make is that they design based on what they

want to build not what Their audience needs to see designing effective visuals requires a level of empathy and an understanding of who your audience is and exactly what they're looking for so here are a few examples including an analyst manager and executive the analyst tends to be someone who wants

detail they like to understand exactly what's going on at a granular level so they're likely to respond well to things like data tables or combo charts with enough detail to support root cause analysis the manager typically wants more summarized data that leads to clear

insights that will help them operate the business for the manager audience it's best to stick with common charts and graphs and only enough detail to support specific insights or recommendations and finally the executive needs highlevel crystalclear kpis to track Business

Health and Topline performance things like kpi cards or very simple charts with minimal detail unless it adds critical context to those metrics so bottom line here is that how you choose to visualize and present data is very much a function of who will be consuming

it analysts or data Specialists may want granular details or complex charts while managers or execs often prefer highle metrics with a focus on clear data driven insights if you enjoyed this content and want to see more we've got a brand new data literacy foundations
